https://www.politico.eu/article/almost-a.text: BRUSSELS — More than 48,300 of the approximately 50,000 people who entered the Spanish exclave of Ceuta from Morocco have returned, a Spanish government official told POLITICO. “Most of the people that came yesterday are now back in Morocco,” said the official, who was granted anonymity to speak freely, adding that the situation was “on the path back to normality.” The influx of migrants could be linked to a recent Spanish court ruling that limited the use of the country’s immediate-return procedure for migrants, the official added. The European Commission said “there are no onward movements towards the European continent or other member states” by the migrants. Advertisement Advertisement

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3rr.text: Image source, Reuters Image caption, Nine people were killed in the shooting at the Greek Orthodox church last month By Ella Kipling Published 2 hours ago A Jordanian court has sentenced three men to death by hanging for carrying out a fatal mass shooting on a church last month. The attack on 23 October killed nine people and injured 34 others who had been attending a Christian funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in Karak governorate. Jordan's Armed Forces said in a statement on Sunday that the men had been convicted of committing "terrorist acts", as well as possessing weapons, "promoting the ideas of a terrorist organisation" and "conspiracy to commit terrorist acts". The three men - two Jordanian brothers and their brother-in-law - fled the scene of the attack and were arrested three days later. They have not been publicly identified. Karak is home to a sizeable Christian community in the Muslim-majority kingdom. CCTV footage from the day of the attack showed three men holding guns approaching and firing on St George's church in the village of Hmoud. Figure caption, Watch: CCTV footage appears to show gunmen near church A second video showed dead and wounded people lying on the ground amid chaotic scenes at the church. It is still unclear why the attackers chose to target that specific church. Shortly after the attack, Jordan's King Abdullah II wrote on X: "The terrorist attack against Karak will be met with the harshest retaliation. "Those who delude themselves into thinking that they can divide Jordanians with their bullets have no chance in the face of our unity." The three men fled the scene of the shooting and were later located inside an abandoned house in Karak governorate, south of the capital, Amman. They refused to surrender and opened fire on security forces, who returned fire and wounded all three of them , the Public Security Directorate said at the time. No security personnel were hurt in the shootout. King Abdullah praised security forces for chasing the suspects "to the very end". The week after the Karak shooting, Jordan struck what its military said were "terrorist organisations" in Syria in retaliation to the church attack. Syrian health officials told state media that five people, including women, children and an elderly man, were killed in the strike on a village in the southern Daraa province. Jordan said its fighter jets had killed and wounded "several terrorists" without giving further details. Jordan said it had co-ordinated with the Syrian government, but Syria said it had not been notified in advance. Executions in Jordan are carried out by hanging. The kingdom previously observed an unofficial ban on executions from 2006 to 2014, and another pause from 2017 until June this year. Back Credit: CASA HOGAR/FAIR USE Fr. Joseph Walijewski was born in Michigan, ordained a priest in Wisconsin, and spent most of his priesthood serving the people of Peru. Copy link Archive article Print article share on : In the midst of Pope Leo XIV's apostolic trip to South America, which includes several days in his adopted homeland of Peru , where the pontiff spent most of his priestly ministry, the Theological Congress of the Vatican’s Dicastery for the Causes of Saints has affirmed the cause of beatification and canonization of a US priest, Fr. Joseph Walijewski. Bishop Gerard Battersby of the Diocese of La Crosse, Wisconsin, released the news in a recent letter : With gratitude to Almighty God, I am pleased to announce that I have been informed that the Theological Congress of the Vatican’s Dicastery for the Causes of Saints has concluded their review for the Cause of Father Joseph Walijewski. This marks a significant milestone and an important step forward in the advancement of the Cause for canonization. The nine members of the Theological Congress carefully examined the documentation and theological considerations associated with the life, heroic virtue, reputation for holiness, and intercessory power of our Servant of God, Father Joseph Walijewski, and unanimously returned a favorable vote, affirming the merits presented for their consideration. With this favorable vote, Fr. Walijewski's cause moves to the "next stage of the process, which involves consideration of the Positio by the Cardinals and Bishops who are members of the Dicastery." After the episcopal review, the cause is then forwarded to the Pope for his final review, which often results in officially declaring an individual " venerable ." Who is Servant of God Joseph Walijewski? Born in Grand Rapids, Michigan, in 1924, Joseph Walijewski wanted to become a priest and travel to South America. While he initially entered seminary studies with the Franciscans at St. Bonaventure Seminary in Sturtevant, Wisconsin, they didn’t think he could ever become a priest. Walijewski couldn’t fulfill the language requirement and struggled with Latin, Greek and French. The Franciscans recommended that he remain a brother for the rest of his life. Not deterred by the rejection, Walijewski sought to become a priest in the Diocese of Grand Rapids. This too ended in rejection, and so Walijewski started sending letters to neighboring bishops, hoping and praying that someone would accept him. Providentially, Bishop Alexander McGavick of the Diocese of La Crosse, Wisconsin, was looking for Polish-speaking priests to serve the numerous Polish immigrants within his diocese. Walijewski was accepted, finished his studies at St. Francis de Sales Seminary in Milwaukee, and was ordained on April 16, 1950. Fr. Walijewski ended up becoming a trailblazer in South America, initially serving in Bolivia. Upon arriving in the country , Walijewski was “ [h]anded a machete by [the local bishop and] joined the bishop in hacking through the jungle until they found a fit place to build a church . 'Build a church here,’ Bishop Brown said ... and the people will come and build their homes next to it.’” Walijewski did exactly that and founded the parish of the Holy Cross in Santa Cruz. Eventually Fr. Walijewski was sent to Peru, where he desired to build an orphanage. St. John Paul II visited El Salvador in 1985 and met Fr. Walijewski while he was there. John Paul II left $50,000 to the bishops to be used for their work with the poor in Peru and they all voted to give it to Walijewski. “Casa-Hogar Juan Pablo II” was built soon after and the orphanage took the Boys Town model as its framework. Fr. Walijewski remained in Peru the rest of his life, dying in there at age 82 from pneumonia in 2006. His cause for canonization was initiated on May 1, 2013, by Bishop William Patrick Callahan of the Diocese of La Crosse, and this latest development provides new hope that Fr. Walijewski will one day be officially known as a saint.
